reader.title: Half-hanging of a thief at Niptown
bases: A group calling itself a 'lynching party' hung an accused thief by the neck short of death and warned that a further offense would bring 'Judge Lynch's death warrant' (A1); no race is given, so whether it falls in an anti-Black scope is doubtful.

The man was hung up 'till he grew black and blue' and survived, so no one was killed (A1); the 'boys' acted as a self-styled lynching party punishing alleged theft, without lawful authority, but their number is not given (A1).
The only account is the White Pine News item (A1); the Eureka Daily Sentinel and Silver State versions are reprints of the same text (A2, A3).

summary.text: The half-hanging of a thief at Niptown was a non-fatal vigilante hanging of an unnamed man accused of petty theft, carried out by a self-described 'half-way lynching party' on or about Tuesday, 27 December 1881.
The man survived, and the local paper that reported it warned that a further offense would bring a real lynching.
According to the White Pine News, the man was a 'petty larceny thief' who had helped himself to several small sums of money belonging to others.
The paper also said that a search of his cabin had turned up a large number of bar-room spoons.
The item gives neither his name nor his race, and it mentions no complaint to officers or arrest.
On the Tuesday before the paper's 31 December issue, 'the boys up at Niptown' seized the man and, in the paper's words, hung him up 'till he grew black and blue.'
They then let him live, which is why the paper called the affair a 'half-way lynching party.'
The item does not say how many took part, where at Niptown the hanging took place, or at what hour.
The paper reported no arrests and no official action, and it warned that the man's 'next offense will be the signal for Judge Lynch's death warrant.'

The White Pine News ran the story as a short, jocular local item headed 'Strung Him Up', treating the man's guilt as fact and closing with a joke that his spoons outnumbered those Butler was credited with taking at New Orleans.

The Eureka Daily Sentinel reprinted it almost word for word on 5 January 1882 among other Cherry Creek items, and The Silver State of Unionville carried it on 6 January in its 'Sagebrush Screenings' column, crediting the Cherry Creek News.
Neither reprint added any detail or comment, and no other account of the hanging appears in the coverage.

accounts.label: Local newspaper item
accounts.gist: The boys at Niptown held a 'half-way lynching party', hanging a petty thief until he was black and blue, and the paper warned that his next offense would bring death.

framing.detail: Headed 'Strung Him Up', the item treats the hanging lightly, calls the man a thief as fact, and presents a future lynching as the deserved 'signal' for a further offense.
Two other Nevada papers reprinted the item nearly word for word, one crediting the Cherry Creek News.
